title: Tulsi (Holy Basil) — Ocimum sanctum
content: Tulsi (Holy Basil / Ocimum sanctum), revered in India as the 'Queen of Herbs', holds supreme status in Ayurvedic pharmacology. Traditional attributes: Rasa (Taste): Katu (pungent), Tikta (bitter); Guna (Qualities): Laghu (light), Ruksha (dry), Teekshna (piercing); Virya (Potency): Ushna (hot); Vipaka (Post-digestive effect): Katu (pungent); Dosha effect: Pacifies Vata and Kapha, slightly increases Pitta if used in excess. Parts traditionally used: Leaves, seeds, and root. Traditional uses: Alleviates respiratory disorders (Kasa, Shwasa), enhances Pranavaha srotas clarity, boosts digestive warmth (Deepana), and relieves microbial distress (Krimihara). Modern Scientific Observations: Clinical trials indicate adaptogenic, immunomodulatory, antimicrobial, and antioxidant properties due to eugenol, rosmarinic acid, and carvacrol compounds.
source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol II

title: Ashwagandha (Indian Ginseng) — Withania somnifera
content: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera), traditionally known for bestowing 'the strength of a horse' ('Ashwa' = horse, 'Gandha' = scent), is classified as a premier Medhya Rasayana (cognitive and rejuvenating tonic) and Balya (strength enhancer). Traditional attributes: Rasa: Tikta (bitter), Kashaya (astringent), Madhura (sweet); Guna: Laghu (light), Snigdha (unctuous); Virya: Ushna (hot); Vipaka: Madhura (sweet); Dosha effect: Strongly pacifies Vata and Kapha. Parts used: Dried roots. Traditional uses: Deeply rejuvenates nervous system (Majja Dhatu), supports restful sleep (Nidrajanana), enhances physical endurance, combats debility, and bolsters reproductive vitality (Shukrala). Modern Scientific Observations: Extensive studies corroborate withanolides as active compounds promoting stress reduction, lowering serum cortisol levels, supporting cognitive function, and modulating neuro-protective pathways.
source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol I

title: Amalaki / Amla (Indian Gooseberry) — Phyllanthus emblica
content: Amalaki (Phyllanthus emblica / Emblica officinalis) is acclaimed as one of the most potent rejuvenative fruits in Ayurveda and the central constituent of Chyawanprash. Traditional attributes: Rasa: Possesses 5 of the 6 tastes—predominantly Amla (sour), with Kashaya (astringent), Madhura (sweet), Tikta (bitter), and Katu (pungent); only lacking Lavana (salty); Guna: Guru (heavy), Ruksha (dry), Sheeta (cooling); Virya: Sheeta (cooling); Vipaka: Madhura (sweet); Dosha effect: Tridosha Shamaka (balances all three doshas, especially pacifies Pitta due to cold potency and sweet post-digestive effect). Parts used: Fresh and dried fruit pericarps. Traditional uses: Rasayana (longevity promoter), Chakshushya (preserves eyesight), Hridya (supports cardiac strength), and promotes hair growth. Modern Scientific Observations: One of nature's densest sources of bioavailable ascorbic acid (Vitamin C), rich in ellagitannins (emblicanin A and B) demonstrating remarkable hepatoprotective, cardioprotective, and antioxidant activity.
source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol I

title: Haridra / Turmeric — Curcuma longa
content: Haridra (Curcuma longa) is celebrated in classical texts for its purifying, anti-inflammatory, and complexion-enhancing qualities. Traditional attributes: Rasa: Tikta (bitter), Katu (pungent); Guna: Ruksha (dry), Laghu (light); Virya: Ushna (hot); Vipaka: Katu (pungent); Dosha effect: Pacifies Kapha and Vata; detoxifies Rakta (blood) and Pitta when used appropriately. Parts used: Dried rhizomes. Traditional uses: Varnya (promotes luminous complexion), Vishaghna (antitoxic/purifying), Kushtaghna (supports skin health), and Pramehahara (supports healthy carbohydrate metabolism). Modern Scientific Observations: Curcuminoids, especially curcumin, are extensively documented in modern biomedical literature for anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, wound-healing, and antimicrobial efficacy. Piperine (from black pepper / Maricha) enhances its bioavailability substantially.
source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol I

title: Neem (Nimba) — Azadirachta indica
content: Nimba (Azadirachta indica), termed 'Arishta' (reliever of sickness), is renowned for its intense bitterness and systemic cooling properties. Traditional attributes: Rasa: Tikta (bitter), Kashaya (astringent); Guna: Laghu (light), Ruksha (dry); Virya: Sheeta (cooling); Vipaka: Katu (pungent); Dosha effect: Highly pacifies Pitta and Kapha; can aggravate Vata if used excessively. Parts used: Bark, leaves, seeds, and root. Traditional uses: Blood purification (Raktashodhaka), management of skin imbalances (Kushta), fever alleviation (Jwarahara), oral hygiene (Danta Dhavana), and antimicrobial cleansing (Krimighna). Modern Scientific Observations: Nimbin, nimbidin, and azadirachtin provide documented antibacterial, antifungal, anti-ulcer, and anti-inflammatory properties.
source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol II

title: Brahmi / Bacopa — Bacopa monnieri
content: Brahmi (Bacopa monnieri), named after Brahma the cosmic creator, is the premier Medhya Rasayana (cognitive and intellect rejuvenator). Traditional attributes: Rasa: Tikta (bitter), Kashaya (astringent), Madhura (sweet); Guna: Laghu (light); Virya: Sheeta (cooling); Vipaka: Madhura (sweet); Dosha effect: Tridosha Shamaka, particularly soothes Pitta and Vata. Parts used: Whole aerial plant. Traditional uses: Enhances Dhi (comprehension), Dhriti (retention), and Smriti (recall); soothes central nervous system agitation, promotes mental tranquility, and improves sleep quality. Modern Scientific Observations: Bacosides A and B cross the blood-brain barrier, facilitating synaptic neurotransmission, promoting cerebral blood flow, and scavenging reactive oxygen species in the hippocampus.
source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol II

title: Triphala — The Classical Three-Fruit Synergy
content: Triphala ('three fruits') is the quintessential polyherbal formulation of classical Ayurveda, consisting of equal parts dried fruit pericarps of: 1. Haritaki (Terminalia chebula): balances Vata; 2. Bibhitaki (Terminalia bellirica): balances Kapha; 3. Amalaki (Phyllanthus emblica): balances Pitta. Combined, Triphala is a master Tridoshic regulator. Traditional attributes: Contains 5 tastes (all except salty); predominantly Kashaya-Tikta with sweet aftertaste; moderate thermal action. Traditional uses: Anulomana (gentle non-habit-forming bowel regulator and carminative), Chakshushya (ocular health), Deepana-Pachana (kindles Agni, clears Ama), and Rasayana (cellular re-nourishment). Modern Scientific Observations: Rich in gallic acid, ellagic acid, and chebulic acid; clinically noted for regulating gut microbiome balance, supporting colonic motility, providing antioxidant defense, and exhibiting prebiotic properties.
source: Ayurvedic Formulary of India (AFI) Part I

title: Guduchi / Giloy — Tinospora cordifolia
content: Guduchi (Tinospora cordifolia), traditionally called 'Amrita' (the heavenly nectar of immortality), is one of the most revered immunomodulatory herbs in Ayurveda. Traditional attributes: Rasa: Tikta (bitter), Kashaya (astringent); Guna: Guru (heavy), Snigdha (unctuous); Virya: Ushna (hot); Vipaka: Madhura (sweet); Dosha effect: Balances all three doshas (Tridoshahara). Parts used: Mature stems. Traditional uses: Rasayana, Deepana, Jwaraghna (dispels chronic fevers), Raktashodhaka (purifies blood), and enhances overall Vyadhikshamatva (vital natural immunity). Modern Scientific Observations: Modern pharmacological evaluations show rich presence of tinosporide, cordifolioside, and diterpenoid lactones that stimulate macrophage activity, enhance humoral immunity, and protect liver and renal cellular integrity.
source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol I

title: Yashtimadhu / Licorice (Jyeshthamadh / Mulethi) — Glycyrrhiza glabra
content: Yashtimadhu (Glycyrrhiza glabra), popularly known in Marathi as Jyeshthamadh and in Hindi as Mulethi, is the premier soothing demulcent and respiratory herb in Ayurvedic medicine. Traditional attributes: Rasa: Madhura (sweet); Guna: Guru (heavy), Snigdha (unctuous); Virya: Sheeta (cooling); Vipaka: Madhura (sweet); Dosha effect: Pacifies Vata and Pitta, and liquefies vitiated Kapha without aggravating it. Parts used: Dried roots and stolons. Traditional uses: Kanthya (improves voice and relieves sore throat), Kasa-hara (relieves dry and irritative cough / khokla), Shwasa-hara (eases bronchial spasms), and Vranaropaka (heals mucosal ulcerations). Classical home remedies pair Yashtimadhu powder with honey, ghee, or warm water for immediate throat soothing and cough alleviation. Modern Scientific Observations: Rich in glycyrrhizin, isoliquiritigenin, and flavonoids exhibiting documented expectorant, antitussive, anti-inflammatory, and mucosal-protective activities.
source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol I

title: Sitopaladi Churna — Classical Formulation for Cough, Cold & Respiratory Balance
content: Sitopaladi Churna is one of the most famous classical polyherbal formulations described in the Sharangadhara Samhita and Charaka Samhita for the management of respiratory ailments (Pranavaha Sroto-roga). Constituents: 1. Sitopala (Rock candy / Mishri) — 16 parts; 2. Vamshalochana (Bamboo manna) — 8 parts; 3. Pippali (Long pepper / Piper longum) — 4 parts; 4. Ela (Cardamom / Elettaria cardamomum) — 2 parts; 5. Twak (Cinnamon / Cinnamomum zeylanicum) — 1 part. Traditional attributes: Balances Kapha and Pitta doshas; Deepana (digestive stimulant), Kasahara (effective against both dry and productive cough / khokla), and Jwarahara (relieves low-grade fever associated with cold). Traditional usage: Taken traditionally with honey and warm ghee or warm milk. Modern Scientific Observations: Piperine from Pippali enhances systemic bioavailability and macrophage phagocytosis, while essential oils from cardamom and cinnamon exert natural bronchodilatory and antimicrobial effects.
source: Ayurvedic Formulary of India (AFI) Part I

title: Shatavari (Indian Asparagus) — Asparagus racemosus
content: Shatavari (Asparagus racemosus), hailed in classical Ayurveda as the premier female reproductive rejuvenative (Rasayana) and menstrual cycle tonic (Stri-Rasayana), translates literally to 'she who possesses a hundred protectors'. Traditional attributes: Rasa: Madhura (sweet), Tikta (bitter); Guna: Guru (heavy), Snigdha (unctuous); Virya: Sheeta (cooling); Vipaka: Madhura (sweet); Dosha effect: Pacifies Vata and Pitta doshas. Parts used: Roots and tuberous root extracts. Traditional uses: Artavajanana (nourishes and balances the female period cycle), Stanya (promotes healthy lactation), Balya (restores stamina), and soothing to Apana Vayu. It eases menstrual cramps by relaxing uterine spasms, relieves premenstrual syndrome (PMS) mood fluctuations, and balances ovarian and hormonal tissues (Artavavaha Srotas). Modern Scientific Observations: Rich in steroidal saponins (shatavarins I-IV), isoflavones, and polyphenols exhibiting estrogen-modulating, adaptogenic, anti-inflammatory, and uterine-tonic actions.
source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol IV

title: Ashoka (Sacred Asoka) — Saraca asoca
content: Ashoka (Saraca asoca / Saraca indica), whose name literally translates to 'sorrow-less', is one of the most celebrated uterine and gynecological tonics in classical Ayurvedic pharmacology. Traditional attributes: Rasa: Kashaya (astringent), Tikta (bitter); Guna: Laghu (light), Ruksha (dry); Virya: Sheeta (cooling); Vipaka: Katu (pungent); Dosha effect: Balances Pitta and Kapha, pacifies Rakta (blood) disorders. Parts used: Dried stem bark. Traditional uses: Stri-roga-hara (reliever of female gynecological and menstrual ailments), Artava-shamana (regulates heavy menstrual bleeding, menorrhagia, and irregular cycles), and Vedanasthapana (eases uterine pain and menstrual spasms). The classical formulation Ashokarishta is widely utilized in traditional wellness for uterine tone and cycle regularity. Modern Scientific Observations: Bark extracts contain proanthocyanidins, tannins, ketosteroids, and flavonoids that demonstrate strong uterine muscle-regulating and hemostatic activities.
source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol I
